HJM Term Structure Model — Project Report

A plain-language walkthrough of the model and what its currently calibrated parameters actually are, generated 2026-09-03 02:37 UTC directly from this repository's data.

What this model does

This project builds a computer model of the entire US Treasury yield curve — not just the handful of maturities the government actually reports (like the 2-year or 10-year rate), but every point in between, evolving realistically through time. It's calibrated on 2,260 daily observations of 11 tenors (from 0.0833-year to 30-year), spanning 2018-01-02 to 2026-08-31.

Getting there happens in two reductions. First, each day's 11-tenor curve is compressed down to just 3 numbers via a curve-shape fit (Nelson-Siegel). Second, those 3 numbers are rotated into 3 statistically independent factors via PCA, ranked by how much of their combined movement each one explains. The rest of this report walks through both steps and what the model does with the result — using the project's own currently calibrated numbers throughout, not illustrative examples.

The raw data: yield curves over time

Each line below is one day's observed Treasury yield curve — the interest rate the government pays, at that moment, for every maturity from a few months out to 30 years. The shape moves around: it flattens, steepens, and occasionally inverts (short-term rates above long-term ones) as the economy and monetary policy change. A single number, like "the 10-year rate," misses almost all of this — which is the whole reason for building a model of the curve rather than tracking one point on it.

Finding the patterns: Principal Component Analysis

Almost all of the curve's day-to-day movement turns out to follow a handful of repeating patterns — commonly described as the whole curve shifting up or down (level), tilting between short and long maturities (slope), and bending in the middle (curvature). Principal Component Analysis (PCA) finds these patterns statistically, ranked by how much of the curve's actual historical movement each one explains.

FactorVariance explainedCumulative
PC159.3%59.3%
PC224.2%83.5%
PC316.5%100.0%

All 3 factors together necessarily explain 100.0% of the variation in those 3 curve-shape numbers — PCA isn't discarding anything here, just rotating them into statistically independent, ranked-by-importance directions. The real dimensionality reduction already happened upstream, fitting 3 numbers to the whole observed curve instead of tracking every tenor independently.

How the factors behave: mean reversion

Each factor doesn't wander off forever — historically, when one drifts away from its long-run average, it tends to drift back. That behavior is modeled as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process, fit separately to each factor's history. Three numbers describe it: how fast it reverts (kappa), what it reverts to (theta), and how much it jitters along the way (sigma) — summarized here as a half-life: roughly how many trading days it takes a displacement to shrink by half.

FactorkappathetasigmaHalf-life (days)
PC10.28 0.6060.924 620
PC21.07 -0.0751.252 163
PC30.86 0.1771.053 204

These are point estimates — the single best-fit number for each parameter, from a standard method (maximum likelihood) that reports no sense of how uncertain that number actually is. The next section addresses that directly.

How sure are we? Bayesian parameter uncertainty

The point estimates above are a best guess from a finite, noisy sample — not a known truth. Instead of fitting one number per parameter, this section fits a distribution of plausible values via MCMC (Markov Chain Monte Carlo, using PyMC), then summarizes it as a posterior mean and a 90% credible interval: the range that plausibly contains the true value given the data and the model's assumptions.

Factorkappa (mean)90% interval Half-life (days)r̂ (convergence)
PC10.31 [0.03, 0.55] 558 1.010
PC20.96 [0.28, 1.60] 182 1.000
PC30.79 [0.17, 1.40] 223 1.000

The r̂ column is a convergence diagnostic — it should sit close to 1.00 for the fit to be trusted; a value far from 1 would mean the MCMC chains never agreed with each other and the numbers above shouldn't be relied on. Note how much wider some of these intervals are than the single point estimate suggests: that width is real information the point estimate alone was hiding. The project's README documents, on the full simulation, how propagating this uncertainty through to simulated future rates widens the predictive range by roughly 5-10%.

Connecting factors back to real rates

A move in one of the abstract factors above has to translate into an actual change in forward interest rates at every maturity. This figure shows exactly that translation: how much a one-unit move in each factor shifts the forward rate at each point on the curve. A factor that loads heavily on short maturities but not long ones, for instance, mostly reflects near-term rate expectations rather than a broad shift in the whole curve.

Putting it together: simulating the future

With the factors' dynamics calibrated, the model can simulate many possible future paths for the whole yield curve — 200 of them here, one year ahead, starting from the most recently observed curve. This isn't a prediction of what rates will do; it's the range of curve shapes that are consistent with how the factors have historically behaved, which is what makes it useful for scenario generation and stress testing rather than point forecasting.

How accurate is this, really?

Everything above describes the pipeline's mechanics and shows what it produces. This section is the only part of the report that checks whether any of it actually works: a walk-forward backtest that refits the whole pipeline at each of a series of past dates using only data available up to that date, simulates forward, and compares the result to what the curve actually did next. Restricted here to this project's held-out test region (2024 onward -- see registry/backtest_spec.py), the only span whose results this project treats as a reportable number rather than something used to help design the model.

Horizon (days)OriginsRMSENaive RMSE Skill vs. naiveCoverage [95% CI]
21320.0028 0.0018-52% 93% [89%, 95%]
63300.0040 0.0034-19% 95% [93%, 97%]
126270.0054 0.0043-24% 99% [97%, 99%]
252210.0066 0.0059-13% 100% [98%, 100%]

Two different questions, two different answers. The model's uncertainty quantification is honest: coverage sits at or above the nominal 90% at every horizon tested. Its point forecast is not consistently better than doing nothing: "skill vs. naive" is the fraction of RMSE the model removes relative to a no-change forecast, and it's negative at most horizons and most maturities (see scripts/run_backtest.py --multi-horizon for the full per-tenor breakdown) -- meaning the median forecast is sometimes further from the truth than simply assuming nothing changes. This is a well-known property of interest rates (and exchange rates): they are close enough to a random walk that beating one with a point forecast is genuinely hard, not a sign of a broken model. Reported as found rather than hidden behind the coverage number alone -- a model can have an honestly calibrated uncertainty band and a point forecast with no real edge at the same time, and conflating the two would overstate what this model can actually do. The confidence interval on coverage also treats each origin as independent, which consecutive overlapping-window origins aren't quite -- see TODO.md.

What this model doesn't do

In the interest of not overstating what's here:

  • This simulation runs under the real-world ("P") measure by default — it describes plausible future curve shapes, not risk-neutral prices a trader could hedge against. A risk-neutral ("Q" measure) mode exists, but the market price of risk it would need is deliberately left at zero rather than calibrated — this project only has spot Treasury yields, not the derivative prices that would be needed to estimate it honestly (see TODO.md).
  • The Bayesian section above fits each factor's uncertainty independently, then (when propagated into simulation) pairs draws across factors somewhat arbitrarily — it is not a sample from a true joint posterior over all factors at once.
  • This is a research and educational model, not a production pricing system — see the README's Scope section.
